title: The Short Guide to Managing Your Boss
author: Managing The Future
summary: A compact, practical five-point guide aimed at anyone who reports to someone. The framing is the useful part: managing up is not flattery and it is not reversing the org chart. It is the recognition that the manager-employee relationship is genuinely two-way and that a lot of the friction, delay, and misunderstanding that makes work harder can be reduced by the person in the subordinate role, unilaterally, without any cooperation from above. The five points are lean and memorable. Know what makes your manager weird, which means investing real attention in the idiosyncrasies that sit at their 90th percentile rather than fighting a personality you did not choose. Deliver no surprises unless it is good news, which translates into proactive weekly updates on likelihood and quality. Internalize their priorities, because whatever their boss is pressing them on is now your top priority too. Make them look really good, which is part of the role whether it sits comfortably or not. And push back smartly, which is the part most guides to managing up get wrong. The author is blunt: if your team agrees with you on everything, they are not providing value. Disagreement framed as service to the manager's own goals is the highest form of upward management. For a primary teacher or EdTech lead, the piece lands cleanly as a checklist for the relationship with a headteacher, principal, or district director. The discipline it imposes is the same as the one it imposes on corporate employees: understand the person you report to, remove their uncertainty about your delivery, speak up with evidence shaped to their style, and make their job easier because you share the consequences of their success or failure.
points: Managing up is a two-way responsibility, not a challenge to authority,it means removing your manager's uncertainty about your delivery and making their job easier.
Understand your manager's 90th percentile traits (their idiosyncrasies) and work with them rather than against them, because predictable reliability across any personality type is valued.
Disagreement framed as service to your manager's goals, backed by evidence, is the highest form of upward management,silent agreement is not providing value.
Weekly proactive updates on likelihood and quality prevent surprises and demonstrate that you share the consequences of your manager's success or failure.
quotes: To say you should “manage your boss” feels backward. Isn’t that like cooking for your chef, or doing your CPA’s taxes? But the manager-employee relationship is interesting in that it really is a two-way street, and more so than ever.

Everyone has personality traits where they’re in the 90th percentile, areas where they’re very different from most people. Maybe they’re extremely detail-oriented or unusually direct. Maybe they process decisions slowly or need to think out loud. To “manage up,” you will need to understand these things about your boss.

Your boss should never wonder if you’re going to deliver. Your goal is to be the most consistent and reliable person on their team. Follow through on commitments, show up prepared, and try to under-promise and over-deliver. Every personality type appreciates that kind of predictability.

If your boss is getting heat from their boss or the board about something, that’s the most important thing in their world, and it should also become the most important in yours. Know what your boss is measured on. Know what keeps them up at night.

Part of your job is to make your boss more effective, and to even help market that effectiveness to the rest of the organization. That means reinforcing the messages that are important to them and noting what the team is currently working on and what’s going well.

Managing up isn’t about flattery or being a yes-man: I used to tell my executive teams that if they agreed with me on everything, they weren’t providing value. When you think something could be done better or when you disagree with the manager, be frank.

Acknowledge their authority while making the case for the course of action you think is best. Frame it as serving their goals, not contradicting them. The best bosses want people who think independently and speak up when it matters.

Managing your boss means understanding that they have a job to do, and you can either make it harder or easier. For both your sakes, choose easier.” Archived from Managing The Future (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
